evidence.quote: This review updates the topical management of seasonal and perennial allergic conjunctivitis (SAC/PAC), the most common forms of ocular allergy, emphasizing the importance of tear film integrity and the potential harm from ophthalmic solution additives.
SAC and PAC are IgE-mediated, often underdiagnosed, and frequently comorbid with allergic rhinitis and dry eye disease.

First-line pharmacological therapy includes topical antihistamines, mast cell stabilizers, and dual-action agents, with recent additions like bilastine 0.6 mg/ml (preservative-free, once daily, co-formulated with hyaluronic acid) and cetirizine 2.4 mg/ml.
However, many older products contain benzalkonium chloride (BAK), a preservative that disrupts the epithelial barrier and may promote dry eye.

evidence.quote: Current first-line outpatient emergency treatment for anaphylaxis relies on intramuscular epinephrine via autoinjectors (EAIs), but undercarriage and underuse are common due to factors like needle phobia, bulky devices, dosing limitations, and training gaps.
This review evaluates human studies on novel nasal and sublingual epinephrine products intended to address these barriers.

Data from phase 1 and 2 studies show that several nasal sprays (ARS-1 2 mg, BRYN-NDS1C 13.2 mg, FMXIN002 3.2 mg, Hikma) and a sublingual film (AQST-109-DESF 12 mg) achieve peak plasma concentrations (Cmax) and times to peak (Tmax) comparable to or better than a 0.3-mg EAI.
For example, ARS-1 had a mean Cmax lower than EpiPen but produced comparable or greater blood pressure increases;
BRYN-NDS1C 13.2 mg yielded higher and more sustained plasma levels than the autoinjector;
